item.content:
HackerJournal holds a special place in my heart, it’s one of the magazines I grew up reading as a kid, diving into its pages to fuel my passion for hacking and technology. For Italian enthusiasts like me, it’s been a true gateway into the world of ethical hacking and cybersecurity.

The Article: “I Know Where You Post From”

In particular, my article, titled “So da dove posti” (I Know Where You Post From), appears on page 36. It details the process I followed to geolocate an individual using only open source intelligence (OSINT) techniques, starting with a single public photo.

This article expands upon the methodology I previously shared in my post How I Solved the Unlock Security OSINT Challenge, where I explained in detail how I solved a similar OSINT challenge. If you’re interested in reading the full solution, you can check out the article for more in-depth insights.

Sharing this methodology is a step toward raising greater awareness about online privacy and the risks of sharing seemingly harmless information online.

Get Your Copy

The January issue (N.275) of HackerJournal is now available for purchase. You can grab your copy here:
👉 HackerJournal N.275 - Sprea Editori

Thank you for your support, and I hope this article inspires others to explore OSINT while being mindful of their digital footprint.

Gratitude

A heartfelt thank you to Sprea Editori and Unlock Security for giving me this incredible opportunity to contribute to such a respected publication.

item.title: How I Solved the Unlock Security OSINT Challenge
item.description: Inspired by the many challenges by Gary Ruddell (LinkedIn Profile), Unlock Security (LinkedIn Profile) has introduced a rather unique OSINT challenge: no contextual information and just a single blurry photo with few visible details. 🔎 The Challenge: Can you determine the location where this photo was taken? Step 1: Using Face Recognition To begin, I used facecheck.id, an online face recognition tool, to identify if the person in the photo appears on any public platform or social media.
item.content:
Inspired by the many challenges by Gary Ruddell (LinkedIn Profile), Unlock Security (LinkedIn Profile) has introduced a rather unique OSINT challenge: no contextual information and just a single blurry photo with few visible details.


🔎 The Challenge: Can you determine the location where this photo was taken?

Step 1: Using Face Recognition

To begin, I used facecheck.id, an online face recognition tool, to identify if the person in the photo appears on any public platform or social media.

The results returned several public profiles with similar facial features. Among them, one matched the original image perfectly.

This individual appears to be the same person. I followed the link to the site where this photo was published, fapello.com, an adult content website.

Under the photo, two nicknames were listed: kat3martynova and katmartynova1. Searching on Instagram, I found her public profile: kat3martynova.

Step 2: Analyzing Instagram Stories

Looking at the Instagram Stories collection titled Адам и Ева, I immediately recognized the blurred objects from the original photo, which I couldn’t previously interpret.

They turned out to be fake apple tree installations represented by glowing red lights.


From the page source code, I copied the title “Адам и Ева” and translated it from Russian to English using deepl.com.


In one of the Instagram Stories, the person enters a venue clearly labeled Adam & Eve, as shown on a sign in the background.

Step 3: Identifying the Venue

Using Google Images, I found multiple photos of the venue. From the available links, it appears to be a nightclub within an adult-only hotel: Adam & Eve Hotel.


Searching for the Adam & Eve Hotel on Google Maps, I located the place.

Step 4: Pinpointing the Exact Spot

Returning to the original photo, I identified some key details that helped me determine the exact spot where the photo was taken:

  1. White speakers at the top (green arrows).
  2. One or more white columns in sequence on the left (yellow arrows).
  3. A mirrored wall starting on the right (blue arrows).

Examining the Adam & Eve Hotel website, in the Gallery section (Gallery Page), I found multiple photos of the hotel’s bars. These images matched the original photo with the same speakers, columns, and mirrored wall.

Finally, using wikimapia.com, I pinpointed the exact spot on the map and identified the bar within the hotel’s structure.

It can now be stated with high certainty that the photo of the individual was taken inside the Bar of the Adam & Eve Hotel, specifically at:

R3X9+R2 Serik District, Antalya Province, Turkey (Google Maps Location).

item.content:
Welcome!

I’m excited to introduce a project I’ve been working on during my preparation for the Offensive Security Certified Professional (OSCP) certification.

On my GitBook, you’ll find:

  • Detailed cheatsheets covering penetration testing methodologies.
  • Useful commands and quick references.
  • Lessons learned and practical tips from my OSCP journey.

The goal is to provide a resource for anyone aiming to tackle and successfully pass this prestigious ethical hacking certification.

What You’ll Find

The guide is structured to cover the key areas of OSCP preparation, with chapters dedicated to:

  • Network Scanning and Service Enumeration: Techniques and tools for identifying vulnerable services (FTP, SMB, HTTP, LDAP, and more).
  • Service Exploitation: Methods for exploiting known vulnerabilities in various protocols and applications.
  • Web Application Attacks: File inclusion, SQL injection, command injection, and more.
  • Privilege Escalation: Techniques to gain full control of compromised Windows and Linux systems.
  • Active Directory: Strategies for attacking, lateral movement, and exploiting vulnerabilities in AD domains.
  • Shells and File Transfers: Approaches for obtaining and maintaining remote access to compromised systems.

Reflections on the OSCP Exam

The OSCP exam is a unique and challenging experience, simulating a real-world network environment containing vulnerable machines. I had 23 hours and 45 minutes to achieve the exam objectives and an additional 24 hours to submit my documentation.

Throughout my preparation, I learned the importance of consistent practice, organization, and maintaining a positive mindset. Despite the difficulties, the journey to OSCP certification has been incredibly rewarding!

Support and Compliance

I’ve created this guide while strictly adhering to Offensive Security’s non-disclosure policies. All information shared is derived from public sources or my personal experiences.

If you find my work helpful, you can support me by buying me a coffee! Every gesture is appreciated and helps me continue creating valuable content for the community.

Explore the Guide

👉 Check out the guide on GitBook

If you’re considering taking on the OSCP challenge or want to deepen your knowledge of ethical hacking, I hope this guide inspires and supports your journey.

Good luck on your path to OSCP certification!

item.content:
PwnDoc <= 0.5.3 - Username Enumeration via Different Responses

CVE Detail

PwnDoc through version 0.5.3 might allow remote attackers to identify disabled user account names by leveraging response messages during authentication attempts.

Vulnerability Summary

Product CVE CVSSv3 Score CWE
PwnDoc CVE-2022-44023 5.3 (Medium) CWE-307

Exploitation Steps

This vulnerability enables username enumeration of disabled accounts in PwnDoc (tested on version 0.5.3 - 2022-07-19) by observing server responses to login attempts.

Example Scenario:

Suppose the following users were registered and subsequently disabled in PwnDoc:

When attempting to log in with one of these disabled accounts, the application responds with a specific error message “Account disabled”:

Client Request and Server Response:

  • Request: Login attempt with a disabled username
  • Response: “Account disabled”

In contrast, when attempting to log in with a non-existent user, the application responds with a different message “Invalid credentials”:

Exploitation Technique:

An attacker can exploit this behavior to enumerate disabled accounts by:

  1. Performing a brute force dictionary attack with a list of potential usernames via POST login requests.
  2. Observing the responses to distinguish between:
    • “Account disabled” (indicating a valid but disabled account).
    • “Invalid credentials” (indicating a non-existent account).

This enumeration can be leveraged to identify accounts that may later be re-enabled by an administrator, increasing the attack surface.

PwnDoc CVE-2022-44022 5.3 (Medium) CWE-307

Exploitation Steps

This vulnerability enables user enumeration in PwnDoc (tested on version 0.5.3 - 2022-07-19 and earlier) by observing web server response times during login attempts.

Example Scenario:

Suppose the following users are registered in PwnDoc:

A brute force dictionary attack can be executed by sending a list of usernames via POST login requests.

  • Long response times: Valid users
  • Shorter response times: Invalid users

Technical Notes:

item.content:
XWiki Platform < 12.8 - Stored Cross Site Scripting (XSS)

CVE Detail

In XWiki Platform before version 12.8, certain fields like “Company” in the user profile editing section are vulnerable to Stored Cross Site Scripting (XSS) attacks due to improper escaping.

Vulnerability Summary

Product CVE CVSSv3 Score CWE
XWiki CVE-2020-13654 7.5 (High) CWE-116

Exploitation Steps

This vulnerability allows an attacker to inject malicious scripts into certain fields (e.g., “Company”) in the user profile section, which are subsequently executed in the browser of any user accessing the page.

Attack Details:

Stored XSS vulnerabilities allow attackers to persistently inject scripts into a trusted application. When unsuspecting users view the affected page, their browser executes the malicious code, which can be used to:

  • Steal cookies or session tokens.
  • Hijack user accounts.
  • Perform unauthorized actions on behalf of the victim.

Steps to Reproduce:

  1. Login as an admin user.
  2. Create a new test user.
  3. Navigate to the user profile page: https://localhost/bin/view/XWiki/
  4. Click the “Edit” button near the Personal Information section.
  5. Insert the following payload in the “Company” field:
<script>alert();</script>
  1. Save the changes and view the profile page.
  2. Observe the XSS execution in the browser.
